records.sourceFile: Quantification of neuromuscular fatigue - What do we do wrong and why.pdf

paper.citation: Place N, Millet GY. Quantification of Neuromuscular Fatigue: What Do We Do Wrong and Why? Sports Med. 2020;50:439-447.
paper.abstract: This opinion paper highlights pitfalls in quantifying neuromuscular fatigue with voluntary and evoked contractions. Problems can arise from the definition of fatigue and the index chosen (for example power vs isometric torque), the delay between exercise termination and testing, the stimulation technique and the way data are analyzed. The authors discuss alternatives proposed in the literature and give best-practice recommendations.
paper.tldr: How neuromuscular fatigue is measured can change the answer: the index chosen, the delay before testing and stimulation settings all bias results. Lab testing should familiarize participants first and combine several fatigue measures.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search, published as a Current Opinion article. It discusses published studies, mainly from the authors' groups, under four headings: the definition of fatigue, single-joint vs whole-body exercise, surrogates of nerve electrical stimulation, and other stimulation, recording and analysis issues.
paper.findings: After a Wingate test, maximal power fell relatively more than isometric MVC force, while the opposite occurred after severe and moderate intensity cycling, so which task looks most fatiguing depends on the index. Typical delays of 1 to 4 min before testing after whole-body exercise allow recovery to begin, and the authors describe a cycling ergometer that permits testing within 1 s with good to excellent reliability. Muscle stimulation through large proximal electrodes gave maximal twitch and M-wave amplitudes similar to femoral nerve stimulation with less discomfort, and TMS outcomes depended on the stimulation intensity used.
paper.limitations: The paper is labeled an opinion piece and does not describe a systematic search. Most supporting evidence comes from the authors' own laboratory studies, and some points rest on unpublished personal data, such as heart rate variability after an ultra-marathon.
paper.practicalImplications: Teams that use MVC and evoked-force testing should familiarize athletes in a separate session, test as quickly as possible after exercise, and combine isometric force with other indices such as maximal power or time to task failure. These are expert recommendations rather than tested protocols.
paper.athleteDev: A sprint power test and an isometric MVC can rank the same fatiguing session differently, so performance staff should not treat any single measure as fatigue. The authors also note that neuromuscular fatigue explains performance only in part.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport and cannot be used to set clearance criteria. Its example that MVC and evoked forces had recovered 16 days after a 166-km ultra-marathon while other signs suggested incomplete recovery is anecdotal.

paper.citation: Sclafani C, Smith P, McHugh T, Crane P. Resident Case Series: The Utility of the Athletic Shoulder Test Using Wireless Portable Force Plates for Measuring Peak Force in NCAA Division One Collegiate Quarterbacks. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2025;20(7):1039-1049.
paper.abstract: This case series explored the feasibility of the Athletic Shoulder (ASH) test using portable force plates to measure upper extremity isometric strength in three NCAA Division I quarterbacks. Testing was done weekly over nine weeks in the Y and T shoulder positions. The dominant shoulder produced greater peak force than the non-dominant shoulder in both positions, and athletes averaged at least 14% of body weight in force.
paper.tldr: Sport-specific isometric shoulder testing on portable force plates was practical to run weekly in collegiate quarterbacks. Dominant-arm force was about 13 to 14% higher than the non-dominant arm, which gives staff a baseline for monitoring.
paper.methods: Case series of three NCAA Division I quarterbacks, the top three on the depth chart and the only scholarship quarterbacks on the roster, with no current or prior upper extremity injury at pre-season screening. Weekly testing before practice on non-game days over nine weeks, using the ASH test in the prone Y (135 degrees abduction) and T (90 degrees) positions on VALD ForceDecks portable force plates, three trials per position, with peak force normalized to body weight and limb symmetry index calculated from dominant to non-dominant arm.
paper.findings: Mean peak force in the Y position was 142.33 N dominant and 128.00 N non-dominant (LSI 1.13). In the T position it was 134.04 N dominant and 119.44 N non-dominant (LSI 1.14). Peak force was higher in the Y than the T position within each arm. Across both positions and arms, average peak force was at least 14% of body weight. The authors report only descriptive statistics.
paper.limitations: Only three athletes from a single team were tested for nine weeks, so the findings cannot be generalized, and no validity, reliability or normative data were established. The authors did not test the athletes on the same day of each week. Standard deviations differ between the text (all trials) and Table 2 (athlete averages), and the text gives a Y-position dominant advantage range of 4% to 16% while Table 2 ratios run from 1.04 to 1.19. The case series has no comparison group and no link to injury or performance outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Force-plate ASH testing in throwing-specific positions is feasible to run weekly within a practice routine. Teams could use a pre-season baseline and in-season comparisons to see whether a quarterback's force falls below their own baseline, but the 14% of body weight figure is only a local reference from three athletes and should not be treated as a normative standard.
paper.athleteDev: For strength and conditioning staff, the ASH test gives a sport-specific measure of shoulder force that can be tracked weekly against each athlete's own baseline. The paper shows feasibility and describes how the team used the data, but it does not show that acting on the data improves performance.
paper.rtp: The paper suggests that force-plate ASH testing could eventually inform return-to-play decisions for overhead athletes, but it does not show this. No athlete in the study was injured or returning from injury, and no criteria for return were tested.

records.sourceFile: Rating of perceived exertion and velocity loss as variables for controlling the level of effort in the bench press exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Varela-Olalla D, del Campo-Vecino J, Leyton-Román M, Pérez-Castilla A, Balsalobre-Fernández C. Rating of perceived exertion and velocity loss as variables for controlling the level of effort in the bench press exercise. Sports Biomechanics. 2022;21(1):41-55.
paper.abstract: The study examined how RPE and velocity loss relate to the percentage of possible repetitions completed in a Smith machine bench press, and whether combining them improves prediction. Seven men completed three repetition-to-failure tests at loads set to target mean velocities of about 1.00, 0.70 and 0.50 m/s. Both RPE and velocity loss showed strong quadratic relationships with %REP, and a multiple regression using both variables fitted better than either alone.
paper.tldr: In seven men doing Smith machine bench press to failure, both RPE and velocity loss tracked the share of possible repetitions completed, and using both gave the best estimate. Coaches can pair the two measures to estimate effort per set, but the equation is specific to this exercise and sample.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study in which seven physically active men completed three repetition-to-failure tests on a Smith machine bench press, at loads set from an individual load-velocity profile to target mean velocities of about 1.00, 0.70 and 0.50 m/s. Mean velocity was measured with a linear position transducer, RPE (Borg 1-10) was reported verbally at set intervals, and quadratic and multiple regressions were used to predict %REP.
paper.findings: Quadratic fits were strong for RPE with %REP (r2 = 0.89) and for velocity loss with %REP (r2 = 0.91). The multiple regression with both variables improved fit (r2 = 0.94, SEE 7.18%), giving %REP = 0.76 x VL + 4.27 x RPE - 2.07. For the separate RPE and velocity loss equations, predicted and actual %REP correlated at r = 0.94 to 0.95 across the 140 observations, with trivial systematic bias and random errors of 9.78% (RPE) and 8.89% (velocity loss).
paper.limitations: The sample is small (n = 7), with mixed training backgrounds that the authors flag as a possible confounder. Findings apply to a paused Smith machine bench press and should not be generalised to free-weight lifts or other exercises. The abstract gives an SEE of 9.85% for the velocity loss model, while the Discussion gives 8.96%, and the same data were used to fit and validate the equation.
paper.practicalImplications: A coach using velocity-based training can ask athletes for an RPE at set intervals and read velocity loss alongside it to estimate how much of the possible repetitions has been completed. The equation should be checked before use with other lifts, other people or free-weight bars.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: For bench press sets, the study supports pairing velocity loss with a 1-10 RPE scale to estimate the share of possible repetitions completed and to control effort. It does not show that controlling effort this way improves strength or performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study tested healthy, physically active men, so it cannot inform return to sport, rehabilitation loading or effort targets for injured athletes. It should not be used to set loads after injury.

records.sourceFile: Ready for impact - A validity and feasibility study of instrumented mouthguards (iMGs).pdf

paper.citation: Jones B, Tooby J, Weaving D, Till K, Owen C, Begonia M, et al. Ready for impact? A validity and feasibility study of instrumented mouthguards (iMGs). Br J Sports Med. 2022.
paper.abstract: This four-phase study assessed the laboratory validity, on-field validity, player feasibility and practitioner feasibility of four instrumented mouthguard systems in rugby league. Laboratory kinematics were compared with a headform reference, on-field events were checked against video, 18 players rated fit, comfort and function, and four practitioners rated usability. Total concordance was high for three systems and low for ORB, on-field performance differed between systems, and player and practitioner ratings favoured HitIQ and Prevent.
paper.tldr: The four mouthguard systems differed widely: Biocore-FRI, HitIQ and Prevent matched the laboratory headform closely, and Prevent gave the best combined on-field performance. Teams should check mouthguard events against video before using the counts for player welfare or research.
paper.methods: Four-phase study. Phase I compared peak linear and angular kinematics from each system with a headform reference at 25 to 100 g. Phase II compared triggered events in 80 player-match observations (51 male players, nine matches) with video verification to calculate positive predictive value and sensitivity. Phase III had 18 players rate fit, comfort and function after two training sessions, and Phase IV had four practitioners complete the System Usability Scale.
paper.findings: Total concordance correlation coefficients were 0.986 (Biocore-FRI), 0.965 (HitIQ), 0.525 (ORB) and 0.984 (Prevent). Positive predictive values were 0.98, 0.90, 0.53 and 0.94, and sensitivity was 0.51, 0.40, 0.71 and 0.75. Counting off-camera and inactive assumed false positives lowered positive predictive values to 0.81, 0.60, 0.37 and 0.89. Player fit was highest for HitIQ (88%) and Prevent (85%), and practitioner usability scores were 83.8 and 80.0 for Prevent and 71.3 and 78.8 for HitIQ (preparation and management), against 51.3 and 50.6 for Biocore-FRI.
paper.limitations: Only one camera view followed the ball, so some events could not be verified and were classed as assumed false positives. Recording thresholds were set by each company and affected sensitivity, and the on-field kinematics were not validated. The authors note that the study may have favoured systems previously tested in the laboratory or used in rugby league, and several authors have ties to Prevent Biometrics.
paper.practicalImplications: When choosing an instrumented mouthguard, staff should weigh false positives and false negatives together rather than one alone, and check on-field events against video before using counts for welfare or research decisions. Kinematic values differ between systems, so peak values from one system should not be compared directly with another's.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Head acceleration counts from these mouthguards depend heavily on the system used, so a monitoring team should pick one system, check its events against video, and avoid comparing counts across brands. The study does not link the data to any performance outcome.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study did not link mouthguard data to concussion diagnosis or return-to-play decisions. The authors state that kinematic data in isolation may not support clinical decisions, so this study cannot show that these devices can guide return to play.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between repeated sprint ability, countermovement jump and thermography in elite football players.pdf

paper.citation: Majano C, García-Unanue J, Hernandez-Martin A, Sánchez-Sánchez J, Gallardo L, Felipe JL. Relationship between Repeated Sprint Ability, Countermovement Jump and Thermography in Elite Football Players. Sensors. 2023;23:631.
paper.abstract: In 20 male professional football players, high hamstring thermal asymmetry (0.2 degrees C or more) was associated with a larger sprint 2 slowdown and lower countermovement jump height after a repeated sprint test. Thigh and calf asymmetries showed no such differences.
paper.tldr: Players with hamstring skin temperature asymmetry of 0.2 degrees C or more jumped lower after repeated sprints in this small study, but their jump drop was not significantly larger. Thigh and calf asymmetry did not separate players.
paper.methods: Twenty male professional players had resting lower-limb thermography (thighs, calves, hamstrings) after 48 h rest, following the TISEM consensus. Players were grouped as low (below 0.2 degrees C) or high (0.2 degrees C or more) asymmetry separately for each muscle group. Each performed three countermovement jumps before and after a repeated sprint test (6 x 30 m, 20 s recovery), analysed with mixed two-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: Thigh and calf asymmetry had no significant effect on any sprint or jump variable (p > 0.05). For hamstrings, the high-asymmetry group had a higher percentage slowdown from sprint 1 in sprint 2 (p = 0.013), while the low-asymmetry group had larger differences from its best sprint in sprints 2 to 4 (p = 0.001 to 0.026). The low hamstring asymmetry group jumped higher after the sprint test (37.23 vs 32.78 cm, p = 0.013, ES = 0.28), with no significant group difference before the test or in jump change.
paper.limitations: Small sample of 20 male players with subgroup sizes not reported. Single thermography session and a low cut-off set by club policy rather than evidence; the authors say a higher cut-off might show stronger relationships. Fatigue was inferred from performance measures, and the non-significant pre-test jump difference (40.80 vs 37.79 cm) may partly explain the post-test difference.
paper.practicalImplications: Hamstring thermal asymmetry may be worth exploring as a monitoring input alongside sprint and jump tests. It should not be used as a fatigue threshold or to change training without replication in larger samples.
paper.athleteDev: Hamstring thermal asymmetry was associated with sprint 2 slowdown and post-sprint jump height in professional players. This is preliminary support for studying thermography as a monitoring tool, not for using it in place of performance tests.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It was done in players without recent injury or pain, and it cannot be used to judge injury status, tissue healing or readiness to return.

records.sourceFile: Relative Motion between the Helmet and Head in Football Impact Test.pdf

paper.citation: Joodaki H, Bailey A, Lessley D, Funk J, Sherwood C, Crandall J. Relative Motion between the Helmet and Head in Football Impact Test. J Biomech Eng. 2019.
paper.abstract: Seven helmet-to-helmet impact configurations were simulated with helmeted crash test dummies. Helmets translated 12 to 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees with respect to the head, and helmet peak linear acceleration was 2 to 5 times the head's. The authors conclude that head motion must be measured independently of the helmet.
paper.tldr: Helmets move noticeably relative to the head during football impacts, so video tracking of the helmet alone does not capture head biomechanics. Head motion needs its own measurement.
paper.methods: Laboratory impact experiment. Two sled systems propelled Hybrid III dummies wearing large Riddell Speed Classic and Schutt Air XP Pro helmets into each other in seven front, side and oblique configurations at 8 to 11 m/s closing speed. Helmet and head kinematics were measured with helmet-shell and head-centre sensor packages and an 18-camera optical motion capture system, analysed from 10 ms before contact to 20 ms after loss of contact.
paper.findings: Helmets translated 12 to 41 mm, mostly downward, and rotated up to 37 degrees relative to the head. Peak resultant linear acceleration of the helmet was about 2 to 5 times that of the head. Peak resultant angular velocity of the helmet ranged from 37 percent less to 71 percent more than the head, depending on the impact condition.
paper.limitations: Crash test dummies, which lack biofidelity in some impacts, rather than human heads or players. Each of the seven configurations was run once with two helmet models, and helmet fit, chin strap tension, hair and friction were not varied. One helmet sensor package failed and one dummy's data were missing for one test.
paper.practicalImplications: Helmet-mounted sensors or video of helmets are not enough to estimate head motion in football impacts; the authors estimate helmet-based angular velocity could be in error by up to 71 percent. Head-mounted or independent head measurement should be used where head kinematics are needed.
paper.athleteDev: Staff using helmet video or helmet-based impact data to estimate head motion should treat it as a measure of helmet movement, not the head, which matters for how impact data are interpreted across football practice and games.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It uses crash test dummies and cannot be used to judge whether an injured player is ready to return.

records.sourceFile: Reliability of three landmine-punch-throw variations and their load-velocity relationships performed with the dominant and nondominant hands.pdf

paper.citation: Omcirk, D., Vetrovsky, T., O'Dea, C., Ruddock, A., Wilson, D., Maleček, J., et al. Reliability of Three Landmine-Punch-Throw Variations and Their Load-Velocity Relationships Performed With the Dominant and Nondominant Hands. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024. (Ahead of print)
paper.abstract: The authors assessed the reliability and load-velocity profiles of three landmine punch throw variations (seated without trunk rotation, seated with trunk rotation, and standing whole body) at three loads with the dominant and nondominant hands in 14 boxers. Most variations were highly reliable, the nondominant hand was as reliable or more reliable, and group-average load-velocity relationships were very strong. Individual data gave more accurate profiles than group averages.
paper.tldr: The landmine punch throw is a reliable unilateral upper-body ballistic test when used across both hands and three loads. Load-velocity profiles should be built and read for each athlete, not compared with a group average.
paper.methods: Fourteen trained boxers completed one laboratory visit. In a quasi-randomised order they performed three repetitions of each of three landmine punch throw variations, at 20, 22.5 and 25 kg, with each hand, and peak velocity was recorded with a GymAware linear position transducer. Intraclass correlation coefficients, coefficients of variation and standard error of measurement were calculated for reliability, and repeated-measures ANOVA was used to compare slopes, intercepts and peak velocity.
paper.findings: Most combinations had good reliability (lower 95% CI 0.75 to 0.89), and the nondominant hand was as reliable as or more reliable than the dominant hand. Group-average load-velocity regressions were very strong (R2 0.96 to 0.99). Slopes and intercepts did not differ by variation or hand. Peak velocity was highest for the whole-body variation, was greater with the dominant hand (mean difference 0.091 m/s), and fell as load increased. The area under the line differed by variation (greatest for the whole-body variation). The abstract states most ICCs exceeded 0.91, but Table 2 shows 8 of 18 ICCs below 0.91 (lowest 0.77, dominant hand), so the table values are reported here.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and its sex and competitive level are not described. The load range was narrow (20 to 25 kg), and the authors note that a wider range could change the profile. The abstract's ICC summary (above 0.91) does not match Table 2, where 8 of 18 ICCs fall between 0.77 and 0.89. The text says the seated without-rotation variation had higher peak velocity than the seated-with-rotation variation, but Table 1 shows the opposite at each load, so the table is used here. Results reflect healthy boxers in one session, not repeated testing over time.
paper.practicalImplications: The landmine punch throw can be used as a unilateral upper-body ballistic test, with both hands and a set of loads. Practitioners should track each athlete's own load-velocity profile over time and compare the two hands within the same athlete, rather than using the group average as a benchmark.
paper.athleteDev: Use the landmine punch throw as a unilateral upper-body power test across both hands at 20 to 25 kg, and keep the same variation and hand in each session. Build individual load-velocity profiles to track progress and check limb asymmetry, rather than comparing athletes to the group average.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy boxers with no injured athletes and no return-to-play criteria, so its reliability values should not be used as return-to-sport thresholds for an injured athlete.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-play criteria based on infrared thermography during anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation in football players.pdf

paper.citation: Escamilla-Galindo V-L, Felipe JL, Alonso-Callejo A, et al. Return-to-play criteria based on infrared thermography during anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation in football players. Biol Sport. 2025;42(2):161-167.
paper.abstract: Descriptive longitudinal study of knee skin temperature asymmetry measured by infrared thermography in 30 football players (male 23, female 7) during rehabilitation and return-to-play after ACL reconstruction, from day 2 to day 365. A linear mixed model with athlete as a random effect was used, and asymmetry decreased over time after surgery, with no significant sex effect.
paper.tldr: Knee skin temperature asymmetry after ACL reconstruction fell steadily over the first year, which may help staff track healing between rehabilitation stages. The study does not show that any temperature value marks a safe return to play.
paper.methods: Thermal images of the anterior legs were taken at days 2, 9, 20, 35, 63, 126, 187, 274 and 365 after surgery, using a FLIR T530 camera and standard room conditions. Knee regions of interest were extracted with ThermoHuman software, and the injured minus healthy knee asymmetry was modelled with linear mixed models (Day and Sex as fixed effects, athlete as random effect), with the best model selected by AIC.
paper.findings: Asymmetry decreased with time after surgery (-0.01 degrees C per day, P < 0.01, Table 2), with a model intercept of 1.92 degrees C. Sex was not significant (estimate 0.14, P = 0.18). The authors report a model-based estimate of 2.52 degrees C at surgery and 1.62 degrees C at day 90, and a final asymmetry of 0.46 +/- 0.13 degrees C, still above healthy-knee values. The study did not record actual return-to-play dates, so the temperature values were not linked to return outcomes.
paper.limitations: The study has no return-to-play dates or reinjury outcomes, and no other rehabilitation or performance measures were collected. Clubs used different rehabilitation protocols, leagues were heterogeneous, and only players who met functional criteria in the first year were included. The abstract states both predictors were significant, but Table 2 shows sex was not (P = 0.18).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can track the injured minus healthy knee temperature asymmetry at set time points after ACL reconstruction, and look for a steady decline over the first year. A single asymmetry value should not be read as a clearance threshold, and combining knee with thigh temperature asymmetry is only proposed by the authors as future research.
paper.athleteDev: Thermography could give performance staff an extra monitoring point in the year after ACL reconstruction, where the study shows a gradual decline in knee asymmetry that was still above healthy-knee values at day 365. It should sit alongside strength, hop and load data rather than replace them.
paper.rtp: The study can support monitoring of knee inflammation and recovery between rehabilitation stages after ACL reconstruction. It cannot be used as a return-to-play clearance criterion, because it has no outcome data linking thermal asymmetry to safe return or reinjury, and the authors did not validate any threshold.
